strengths: Rigorous theoretical foundation: The paper provides a detailed ELBO surgery (Proposition 1 and Corollary 2) that clearly explains distribution matching in joint and conditional spaces, clarifying why standard mixture-based bounds suffer from an irreducible gap due to modality-specific variation.

Insightful information-theoretic perspective: The decomposition into marginal and conditional rate-distortion terms (Lemma 7 and Corollary 8) provides a principled explanation of empirical trade-offs, particularly why mixture-based bounds favor cross-reconstruction at the expense of joint log-likelihood and full reconstruction.

Principled integration of permutation invariance and equivariance: The paper generalizes multi-modal fusion beyond heuristic Product-of-Experts (PoE) and Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) by employing DeepSets and Set Transformers, and elegantly extends this to private-shared latent structures via permutation equivariance.

Thorough empirical evaluation: Experiments span controlled linear Gaussian models, non-linear identifiable benchmarks with ground-truth latent recovery (MCC), and the standard MNIST-SVHN-Text benchmark, with careful capacity controls (e.g., PoE+, MoE+) and ablation studies across hyperparameters.
weaknesses: Incremental core variational objective: The proposed objective effectively combines a marginal ELBO on an observed subset with a conditional ELBO on the complement. While formalizing this for arbitrary masking subsets under general distributions is useful, the core formulation closely mirrors existing ideas from Wu & Goodman (2019) and Latent Neural Processes.

Increased computational overhead: Training requires two separate encoder passes and latent samplings per training instance ($z_S \sim q_\phi(z|x_S)$ and $z_M \sim q_\phi(z|x)$), which roughly doubles the encoding computation compared to standard uni-modal encoder passes.

Mixed empirical performance on downstream metrics: While the proposed method consistently achieves superior joint and marginal log-likelihoods, it does not consistently outperform mixture-based baselines on generative coherence or linear latent classification accuracy on MNIST-SVHN-Text.

Minor presentation and citation typos: There are forward-referencing issues in the main text (e.g., Remark 3 references 'Corollary 19' which appears in Appendix A, rather than Corollary 2 in the main body; Section 3.2 references equation '(3.1)' which is unnumbered).

strengths: Principled Theoretical Formulation: The paper provides a clear and rigorous theoretical grounding for the proposed bound via multi-modal ELBO surgery (Proposition 1, Corollary 2), formalizing how the combination of marginal and conditional bounds avoids the inherent variational gap of mixture-based objectives and characterizes exact distribution matching.

Well-Motivated Aggregation Architectures: Replacing fixed, restrictive pooling operators (such as PoE and MoE) with learnable permutation-invariant and permutation-equivariant networks (SumPooling and Set-Attention) effectively resolves representational bottlenecks while cleanly handling both shared and modality-specific/private latent variables.

Connection to Identifiability and Rate-Distortion: The manuscript nicely connects multi-modal inference to non-linear identifiability (treating subsets as auxiliary conditioning variables) and provides valuable insights into rate-distortion trade-offs across modalities.

Thorough and Honest Experimental Analysis: The empirical evaluation covers analytical linear setups, non-linear identifiable benchmarks, and standard vision-text data (MNIST-SVHN-Text), carefully controlling for parameter counts (e.g., PoE+ / MoE+ baselines) and transparently analyzing where the bound excels (LLH, full reconstruction) and where mixture bounds retain advantages (cross-reconstruction).
weaknesses: Computational Overhead: Training requires evaluating encodings and drawing latent samples from both the subset posterior $q_\phi(z|x_S)$ and full posterior $q_\phi(z|x)$ for stochastically sampled subsets $S$, leading to higher training times and memory usage compared to simpler objectives. A concrete wall-clock runtime comparison across different modalities $M$ would clarify scalability.

Cross-Modality Generation Trade-offs: While the proposed objective achieves higher joint and marginal log-likelihoods and full reconstruction quality, mixture-based bounds remain superior in some conditional cross-reconstruction metrics and latent classification accuracies (as visible in Tables 6 and 13).

Benchmark Diversity: Experiments on realistic data are limited to the established MNIST-SVHN-Text dataset. Validating the approach on higher-resolution multimodal benchmarks or genuine biological data (such as the multi-omics settings highlighted in the introduction) would substantially strengthen empirical significance.

Minor Notational Inconsistencies: In Section 2.1 (pages 6, 7, and 8), the text repeatedly cross-references 'Corollary 19' from the appendix instead of 'Corollary 2' from the main text. There are also occasional minor typos (e.g., 'inditerminancy' on page 22).

strengths: Principled Theoretical Formulation: The paper addresses a well-known limitation of mixture-based multi-modal VAE bounds (i.e., the irreducible conditional entropy gap identified by Daunhawer et al., 2022) by formalizing a joint-conditional decomposition bound (LS + L\S). The ELBO surgery in Proposition 1 and the rate-distortion interpretations in Section 2.2 provide valuable conceptual insights into how different multi-modal objectives balance marginal and conditional dependencies.

Flexible Permutation-Invariant / Equivariant Aggregations: Moving beyond standard Product-of-Experts (PoE) and Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) to learned set functions (DeepSets, Set Transformers) is mathematically well-motivated and allows the model to support non-Gaussian variational families (e.g., Gaussian mixtures) and private latent variable decompositions in a natural way.

Thorough Connections to Identifiability: The paper provides a clear link between multi-modal conditioning and recent non-linear ICA / iVAE identifiability results (Proposition 15), supported by controlled experiments tracking the Mean Correlation Coefficient (MCC) on synthetic identifiable systems.

Extensive Experimental Exploration: The empirical validation spans linear generative models with analytical likelihoods, non-linear identifiable latent variable setups, and the standard MNIST-SVHN-Text benchmark across multiple ablation axes (varying beta, shared vs. private latents, and different aggregation backbones).
weaknesses: Format and Length Issues: The manuscript is formatted as a 65-page journal paper with 26 pages of main text. For an ICML submission (typically 8–9 pages of main text), this drastically exceeds standard conference constraints. The narrative is often overly verbose and needs substantial condensation to highlight the core contributions within conference limits.

Incomplete and Unpolished Appendix Sections: Several sections in the appendix are unfinished or contain broken cross-references. For instance, on page 55, Sections L.3, L.4, and L.5 are empty section headings without text. On page 63, there are missing citations/broken references ('as in [empty line] and follow...'). Furthermore, Remark 3 in the main text cites 'Corollary 19' (which appears in the appendix) rather than Corollary 2.

Limited Originality of Individual Algorithmic Components: While the synthesis is thorough, the individual building blocks are well-established: the bound (LS + L\S) is an extension of the conditional ELBO / latent neural process formulation and Wu & Goodman (2019), and DeepSets/Set Transformers are standard off-the-shelf set architectures.

Mixed Downstream Empirical Gains: While the proposed bound and aggregation models consistently improve joint and marginal log-likelihood estimates, they do not uniformly improve cross-modal coherence or latent classification accuracy (as shown in Table 6, Table 8, and Table 13). In several instances, mixture-based bounds remain superior in cross-reconstruction and downstream representation classification, indicating that the likelihood gains come at the expense of other desirable multi-modal attributes.

Computational Overhead: Training requires drawing samples from both the subset posterior q(z|x_S) and the full posterior q(z|x) for each update, roughly doubling the stochastic gradient sampling overhead relative to standard ELBOs, in addition to the extra parameterization and compute required by transformer/deep set aggregators.
